extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political theory, policymakers, and those studying democratic institutions
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating democratic government and majority power
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations for judging democratic institutions, the effects of majority rule, and institutional design choices (stability, checks, popular participation). Useful for analyzing strengths, weaknesses, and trade-offs of democracy, especially the U.S. model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political engagement of the whole community
rubrics_metrics.description: In democratic republics the whole community is engaged in melioration and public life rather than only a portion or a single class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: neighborhood meetings to build churches, elect representatives, district delegates consulting on local improvements, laborers leaving work to deliberate on roads or schools; women attending public meetings; societies (e.g. temperance) formed to address social ills. The text emphasizes ubiquity of political activity — meetings, debating clubs, and constant public discussion — as a characteristic and a benefit of democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy produces ceaseless agitation and social activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic government introduces a ceaseless political agitation that pervades social intercourse and stimulates improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the people may often conduct public business poorly, participation extends their ideas, self-respect, and activity. The author regards this restless energy as possibly the greatest advantage of democracy because of what it causes to be done, even if many projects are imperfectly executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of democracy depends on social aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of democratic government should depend on the chief aims of society — e.g., cultivation of genius and renown versus provision of comfort and necessities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the aim is to 'confer a certain elevation upon the human mind' and foster genius, arts, and heroic virtues, democracy may be an uncertain guide; if the aim is to promote comfort, peace, and equalized conditions of enjoyment for individuals, democratic institutions are well suited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy indirectly fosters commercial and practical activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic institutions (joined with local conditions) are an indirect cause of commercial activity: people learn to promote commerce through legislative experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The effect is indirect (not produced by laws themselves) — democratic participation teaches citizens to mobilize and promote commerce by experience derived from legislation and public deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute sovereignty of the majority
rubrics_metrics.description: The very essence of democratic government is the absolute sovereignty of the majority: in democratic states nothing is capable of resisting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most American constitutions have increased this natural strength by artificial means. The claim sets the baseline for evaluating other institutional consequences and risks associated with majority rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional designs that amplify majority power (short terms, direct elections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Electing legislators directly and for very brief terms, and drawing both houses from the same class and nomination methods, increases the influence and rapid replaceability of legislative bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: legislators subject to daily passions of constituents, rapid and irresistible modifications of legislatures, legislature entrusted with almost all authority; judicial and executive independence weakened (e.g., judges' stipends subject to legislative regulation). These design choices increase democratic mutability and majority dominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom of pledged delegates and constrained representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Electors sometimes impose a line of conduct on their delegates, obliging them to fulfill positive commitments and effectively binding representatives to voters' instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This custom functions like direct majority deliberation in the market-place and can nullify representative independence; it is cited as a practice that further strengthens the majority's control over government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral authority of the majority rests on belief in collective wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority's moral authority is partly based on the notion that collective numbers imply greater intelligence and wisdom than individuals, applying the theory of equality to intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This belief (that interests of many should be preferred to few) helps explain respect for majority rights. Its sway varies with party dynamics and social circumstances; time and continued enforcement consolidate its moral power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instability (mutability) of laws inherent in democracy and exacerbated by majority power
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic governments tend to have mutable laws because men are raised to power in rapid succession; this mutability is amplified by the authority and means of action given to legislatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the U.S., omnipotent legislatures plus rapid turnover mean laws and constitutions are frequently amended and laws change often. Example: many American constitutions amended within thirty years and voluminous legislative acts (e.g., Massachusetts). Instability affects both legislation and administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energetic but less persevering social improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: In America social meliorations are undertaken with zeal and activity but often lack perseverance and continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: prison reform — new penitentiaries built rapidly while old prisons were neglected and conditions worsened. The majority's fleeting attention can accelerate some improvements but cause neglect elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyranny of the majority and need for securities
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlimited power of the majority contains the germ of tyranny; liberty is endangered when the predominant power is unchecked by obstacles that moderate its vehemence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asserts that unlimited power is inherently dangerous and that democratic institutions of the U.S. are problematic not for weakness but for their overpowering strength and inadequate securities against abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of institutional checks: independent legislature, executive, judiciary
rubrics_metrics.description: Precautions must be taken to control sovereign power: a legislature that represents the majority without being its slave; an executive retaining some uncontrolled authority; and a judiciary independent of the other two powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these conditions are met, a government can remain democratic without incurring tyrannical abuse. The absence of such checks in the U.S. is identified as a key flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical lack of redress when majority is unjust
rubrics_metrics.description: Where all public authorities (public opinion, legislature, executive, militia, jury, judiciary) are dominated by the majority, individuals or minorities wronged have few, if any, avenues for effective redress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: Baltimore 1812 mob attacking a newspaper; freed blacks legally allowed to vote but deterred by majority violence and prejudice. Even when laws exist, the majority may be able to break or subvert them in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impossibility of a stable 'mixed government' without a predominant principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of a perfectly mixed government (balancing several principles equally) is a chimera; some social power will always predominate and must be moderated by obstacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: England appeared mixed but in practice aristocracy preponderated. The point guides evaluation of constitutional design: seek effective checks knowing one principle will dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between tyranny and arbitrary power
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyranny can be exercised by means of the law (not arbitrary), while arbitrary power may be used for the public good and not be tyrannical; tyranny commonly employs arbitrary means but does not require them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conceptual distinction helps classify abuses of power and assess whether an action is tyrannical or merely arbitrary; it bears on whether public officers' discretionary actions are legitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncontrolled majority increases arbitrariness of public officers
rubrics_metrics.description: The unlimited power of the majority affects the arbitrary authority exercised by public officers and the actual liberty left to them within their sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The excerpt implies that when the majority predominates unchecked, public officers' discretion may either be co-opted or exercised arbitrarily in ways that reflect majority will rather than legal or constitutional constraints.
